utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we -- first of all, good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I did understand have the videolink, which is already set up, that there was some question about how we would proceed. We have a few matters to deal with - that will take most likely not more than five minutes - before we start hearing the evidence of the witness, which is called today by the Defence. So I'll deal with those first. The first one is -- deals with the evidence of the present witness. With regard to the number of associated exhibits tendered through Jose Cutileiro, the Chamber reiterates that the Defence -- to the Defence that it should not be flooded with associated exhibits and recalls its preference for documents to be tendered during the witness's examination in court or through a videolink. The Chamber therefore invites the Defence to reduce the number of associated exhibits it is tendering through the witness. That is one matter. Then there is another matter which we have to deal with in private session; therefore, the audio link should be discontinued at this moment. It will not last for very long, if I understand well. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd first like to establish whether the videolink is functioning well. Could the representative of the Registry at the videolink location tell us whether he can see us and whether he can hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, good morning, Your Honours. We can see and hear you quite clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see you and we hear you as well. Before I'll invite the witness to make a solemn declaration, I'd first like to know who are present at the videolink location.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours, to my extreme left is Ms. Cristina Moniz, who is a representative of the Government of Portugal, she is here pursuant to the oral order of the Chamber; and then to my left is the witness; and it's myself. And we have technical assistance in the adjacent room in the event that we need to call them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. First of all, Ms. Moniz, welcome in this courtroom, as you are a representative of the Portuguese government. The Chamber expects you not to intervene in the examination of the witness, but you are there as an observer, I take it, unless you would have any other perception of what your role would be and then we would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MONIZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then, Mr. Cutileiro, we'll now proceed and hear your testimony. Before you give testimony, Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration. If it would be difficult for you to stand, please remain seated; otherwise, please stand and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cutileiro. Mr. Cutileiro, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll soon see him on your screen, if you don't see him already. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to first state your full name, first and last, so it can be entered into the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Jose Cutileiro.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And also for the record, is it correct that you are here today pursuant to a subpoena issued by the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I am because if I had not been subpoenaed, I don't think I would have come --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: -- for reason of a general nature. I think that people who have act as mediators, so to speak, in what we usually call peace negotiations should not be called as witnesses if after that for some reason some of court cases arise, I don't think it's satisfactory that we be called as witnesses, but we -- once I have been subpoenaed, here I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I appreciate that. Now today I will have some questions for you and I want to make sure that if you do not understand a question or do not hear a question, you please let us know so I can repeat or rephrase that question. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And since we will both be using the English language, it is important that we pause between question and answer and vice versa so that the court reporter and interpreters can do their job. Is that also understood?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then we will begin and I will first ask you: Have you ever testified previously before the ICTY Tribunal in any other trials?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I did. In 2012 I was again subpoenaed and I testified in the case of Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, sir, did you have an opportunity to give a written witness statement in the -- to the Court in the Karadzic trial?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I would call up in e-court 1D04306. And, sir, I hope the Court Officer over there can give you a copy in paper.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, this is titled as a witness statement of yourself. Can you tell us if you remember giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can turn together to the very last page of the same, both in e-court and in the paper hard copy, in the bottom right corner there is a signature. Can you tell us if you recognise whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look to the left of the signature, there appears to be a date in 2012, which I believe to be 11 Roman numeral IV, 2012?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does that date -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does that date reflect the date you remember signing this statement for the Karadzic trial?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, and I always write the month in Roman characters so there's no doubt that I did date that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank, you, sir. Now, Ambassador, have you received a copy of this statement in its entirety to review the same prior to today to see if everything is accurate and correct in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to perform that review, to see if any corrections are necessary?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there's no -- nothing is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just look at one paragraph together first.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 30 and that is to be found on page 4 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if may direct examination to the last document listed in that paragraph, that is --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry. That, I think, is not quite right because the -- the last letter was not from Dr. Karadzic to me, but from me to Dr. Karadzic if I remember rightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think are you correct, sir, and that is in our case 1D4314, that letter dated 23 July 1992, which as you say was sent to Karadzic by you. Now, apart from this one correction that we have now gone through as to paragraph 30 of the witness statement, do you stand by the remainder of the witness statement as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, if I were to ask you the same questions today about topics in the statement would your answers be essentially the same in substance as we find in the written statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you've just been asked to give a solemn declaration to tell the truth. Can you tell us are the statements in your written statement truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, except for the point we have just went on about, the Karadzic's letter and not my letter -- or, rather, my letter not Karadzic's letter to me. I re-read the statement and I think that's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank, you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D04306 as a public Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit Number D1371, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would read a short public summary of the witness statement for purposes of letting the public know what is contained therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Cutileiro informed about the purpose of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke about with him and indeed it's the same procedure that was in the prior proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then listen to the summary, which is not the evidence but which is just to inform the public about the content of the statement of Mr. Cutileiro. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness joined the foreign service the Portugal in 1974. Ambassador Cutileiro has served in a number of positions since that time, including as Permanent Representative of Portugal to the Council of Europe; as ambassador to, first, Mozambique, and, later, South Africa; as head of the Portuguese delegation to the Stockholm Conference; as political director to the foreign ministry; and in 1992 as special advisor to the foreign minister; in 1994 he became Secretary-General of the Western European Union; and in 2001 to 2004, he was Special Representative of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights for Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia and Montenegro. In February 1992, Lord Carrington, Chairman of the European Commission's Conference on the former Yugoslavia, asked Ambassador Cutileiro to chair talks on the future constitutional arrangements for Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Ambassador participated in several rounds of talks and served in this capacity until 14 August 1992. As a result of the talks, on 18 March 1992, the parties agreed to a Statement of Principles which provided, inter alia, for a state composed of three constituent units within the existing borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A working group was to be established to define the territory of the constituent units, while a map was annexed to the statement which showed the relative majority in each municipality and would be basis of the work of the working group. The Statement of Principles was reached after long and intense negotiations. The Bosnian Serbs agreed in the statement and committed to having religious and ethnic minorities in their constituent unit and respecting the rights of the same, as it was agreed to by all parties and was supposed to be a basis for further negotiations which were, indeed, held. During the period after the Statement of Principles was agreed to, the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs wanted further negotiation on unresolved issues while the Bosnian government leaders dragged their feet. Shortly after the parties agreed to the Statement of Principles, the witness began to hear President Izetbegovic was disavowing his agreement in public statements. In June 1992, the Bosnian government formally rejected the Statement of Principles. The Ambassador's statements also goes through some notes of meetings with Ambassador Okun and others, which he states accurately reflect what he said and believed. Examples are that Izetbegovic is a liar and very untrustworthy. He always goes back on what he agreed to. All sides lied but the Serbs lied the least. On 28 May 1992, the ambassador received a letter from Momcilo Krajisnik of the Serbs, noting that a Muslim broadcasting team was on the spot right after the killing on Vase Miskina Street and stating: "If there is a good will to investigate, it is possible to reach the truth through ballistics and medical expertise." Shortly after the shelling of persons at a bread queue in Vase Miskina Street, the Ambassador spoke with a Portuguese army artillery officer who had participated in the investigation of this shelling and was convinced that the shell had come from the position where the Bosnian government had their positions. Ambassador Cutileiro states that it is a tragedy that peace was not achieved throughout the Statement of Principles negotiated in March 1992. A comparison of the map annexed to the Statement of Principles, and that which is part of the Dayton Agreement, shows that after three and a half years of war, the result was about the same. Countless lives could have been saved. President Izetbegovic and his aides were encouraged to scupper the deal prevented by the Statement of Principles and to fight for a unitary Bosnian state by well-meaning outsiders who thought they knew better. And that concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I do have some additional follow-up questions you. If we can first turn to the first page of the statement in both the paper copy and the e-court and if we can look at paragraph number 6, and here you state: "On 2 March 1992, I received a letter from the Bosnian Serb leaders requesting that the conference carry on as soon as possible, 'in view of the unfortunate events in Sarajevo and throughout B and H.' The letter said that the 'unhappy events' were triggered by President Izetbegovic's statement that transformation into three constituent units was out of the question, and the attack of the Serb father of the groom at a wedding party." At the time of this letter from Karadzic, that is, 2 March 1992, had Izetbegovic conveyed to either you or any of the other negotiators his position that transformation to the three constituent units was out of the question?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Not to me. I don't know about others. Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, generally how would you describe Izetbegovic's stance in these negotiations that led to the Statement of Principles?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Well, like all -- the three parties tried to get as much as each of them could to their own side, but -- and we discussed -- we started discussing in early February. We made some progress in Lisbon at -- a bit later. The meetings were held alternatively in Sarajevo and in -- in Lisbon. At the time Portugal had the Presidency of the European Community. By the way, it's a conference of the European Community, not the European Commission, that Lord Carrington chaired. But we -- so like in other negotiations of this kind, it was just talking. There were things that were easier to some -- than to others, but at the table Izetbegovic went along and we had a joint meeting on the evening of the 17th which finished only on the early morning of the 18th of March with everybody present. I mean, the -- Izetbegovic and his foreign minister; and Karadzic and Koljevic was there since; and on the Croat side Mr. Bubanj was also there. So up to that moment, in the talks, I don't think you could say that they were very different from any other talks of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if we could turn to page 2 of the statement in both the hard copy and in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention to paragraph 11 in the middle of the page, and here we are talking about the Statement of Principles --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- that was agreed to. And you mention a working group that was to be established to define the territory of the constituent units. Who was supposed to make up that working group and be its members?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Representatives of the three sides in the Bosnian talks which, if I may remind the Court, at the time the three sides were also part of a -- were in a coalition government of Bosnia. It was not talks between the government of Bosnia and others. It was the three of them where were in the coalition of the government of Bosnia at the time. But besides them, we had a hope that the European Commission would be able to provide some experts -- that would be some specialists in community problems, in geography; but unfortunately, the European Community did not provide such experts, and that particular committee was never set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, may I take it, it was a slip of the tongue when you referred to paragraph 11, where paragraph 13 seems to be more in line with what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I meant to say, starting at 11 and going to 13. You're correct. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say the European Community did not provide such experts. Do you know any reason why not or -- or how did that occur?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It was not a deliberate intention of the European Community not to provide them. It was just this one was one particular matter that was being discussed in which the European Community were involved. These things are not easy to find -- these people are not easy to find. It is not easy to organise that. There was at the time - and I don't think if there is nowadays - an international organisation or a -- or even some kind of ad hoc arrangement that would provide on request this kind of expertise. So we didn't manage to do it in couple of weeks that or -- if you want a month or so. And by then, then things had deteriorated enough to go on proceeding, trying to get it. I regret it. I think it would have been good if we managed that because that might have kept the parties more committed to what they had agreed, but that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, the Statement of Principles that was -- that was agreed to in 18 March 1992, was it called by any other names perhaps in the media?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Other names? The Carrington-Cutileiro Agreement or -- what sometimes may have been said is the agreement was an agreement on principles, and I suppose perhaps that sometimes in the media that did not come as clearly as that. But I don't know what -- what do you have in mind? Do you have any other labelling for the thing that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've explained exactly what I was asking about, so that's perfect, sir. Now, if we could turn to the third page of your statement in both of hard copy and e-court, and I propose to look at paragraph number 19 on the top of the page. And here it is said that Izetbegovic began disavowing the Statement of Principles in the Bosnian media and that the Bosnian government formally rejected the Statement of Principles in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction, first, of the negotiators upon getting this information that Izetbegovic was disavowing the Statement of Principles; and then later that the government side rejected the Statement of Principles?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: The first I heard of it was shortly after the agreement, and following up on things that Izetbegovic had said before, notably that he didn't believe that an arrangement of that kind, that the -- he considered some kind of confederation of sorts would be feasible. He didn't believe -- that was his feeling at the beginning of the talks but then he agreed on the statement. Then I began hearing, in part, from the Serbs, the Serbs that came to the talks but also from people that were in Sarajevo at the time, that to the local media Izetbegovic said that a thing like that could never work, or words to that effect. I have not -- I was not shown precise quotations. I remember going back to him and asking him if he still accepted the principles, and he always told me that he did. He never told me that he himself - in the framework of these conversations - would renounce or reject them; and then in June they did reject formally, if you wish. But until then, on one side, I heard that he could speak publicly against them to Bosnian media, but to me and to other people directly involved in the conflict, he never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the Serbs and Croats that were participating in the negotiations upon the first hearing that Izetbegovic was disavowing the statement and then later when it was rejected by that side?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: On the first, when they first heard some -- I think they did -- they were among the people who told me that that these were statements made to the press. But, you see, trust was not really a commodity in -- available in great quantity in those talks. The three sides suspected each other very strongly; and the fact that we have managed to get agreement, we thought, was a good sign that they were improving in their attitude towards each other. The fact that they were in coalition in government indicated that they could do together something things even if they didn't trust each other very much. But for them, for Serbs and Croats, this was another illustration of Izetbegovic's duplicitous nature as they saw it from -- and these were the talks I had, I mean, on that matter. As I say, Izetbegovic always told me that he may have said this or that, but -- but he was keen on the conversation. He even came to Lisbon once, I remember, and he participated directly on the drawing of some limits in one map on the basis of the Statement of Principles. So he -- he did -- to me, to the conference, he went on working as if it were possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you and the other negotiators have any explanation or reasoning that you could come to understand why Izetbegovic and the Bosnian government side had disavowed and rejected the Statement of Principles?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Well, I think that it's not unusual in politics that you tell your backers one thing and you tell other people another thing. And we were -- we will to deal with what we had. And what we had was agreement on the 18th of March, and from Izetbegovic who was the leader of the Bosnian side - and was also the president of the country at the time - the firm commitment that it would go on. He might have to satisfy or to appease some of his followers, I don't know. But that was all it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look on the same page at paragraph 20, and I'd like to focus on the first part of paragraph 20 that says: "During the period after the Statement of Principles was agreed to, the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs wanted further negotiations on the unresolved issues while the Bosnian government leaders dragged their feet." And I'd like to ask you if you could please explain or perhaps give an example of what you mean here when you say that the Bosnian government leaders dragged their feet.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Look, if you have the public statements being made and then I had to go and ask Izetbegovic and he would tell me to -- basically to not pay attention to that and pay, rather, attention to what he told me, that -- there were some doubts obviously in the commitment of the -- of the Bosnian side - Bosnian in the sense of the Muslim side at the time as we said - to the -- to the pursuance of the work so that we can -- could move from principles to a final agreement, and this was evidently felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can now turn again to the last page in both the hard copy and in e-court, and I'd like to spend some time discussing paragraph number 35, the last paragraph. And here you are again talking about the Statement of Principles, and you say: "In a letter to "The Economist" in December 1995, I wrote that: "'After several rounds of talks our 'principles for further constitutional arrangements for Bosnia-Herzegovina were agreed by all three parties (Muslim, Serb, and Croat) in Sarajevo on March 18th, 1992, as the basis for future negotiations. These continued, maps and all, until the summer when the Muslims reneged on the agreement. Had they not done so, the Bosnian question might have been settled earlier, with less loss of (mainly Muslim) life and land. To be fair, President Izetbegovic and his aides were encouraged to scupper that deal and to fight for a unitary Bosnian state by well-meaning outsiders who thought they knew better.' "I believed this to be true then and believe it to be true now." Can you explain to us why it is that you consider that President Izetbegovic and his aides were encouraged to scupper the deal?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: For instance, high diplomat from the State Department early in April that year, came to Sarajevo. And in talk -- he was received by Izetbegovic and he advised Izetbegovic to not accept the three-partite plan that we had. He suggested that if they wanted to have some constituent units, then to have more than three. And the -- but he strongly advised him not to accept the -- the three -- or the three were not there by chance or by some arithmetic reason. It was because they constitute the three constituent peoples as they had in their constitution of the country. So the fact that a high American official advised Izetbegovic not to accept that plan seems to me sufficient to make me write to "The Economist" at the time what I did. They were encouraged to scupper that deal and fight for a unitary Bosnia. I believe -- as I put in my statement in -- three years ago, I believed this to be true then and believe it to be true now and I still believe it to be true. And if you read a recent publication, for instance, European Council on Foreign Relations - it's a short booklet, very, very little - by Carl Bildt and he starts by saying exactly the same. He starts by saying that the -- what he calls the Carrington-Cutileiro Plan, if it had been accepted and if it had been put into action, many thousands of lives would have been saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, what is the basis of your knowledge of this involvement of an American officer from the State Department in advising Izetbegovic to reject the three -- tripartite agreement of the Statement of Principles? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: At the time -- at the time the American ambassador in Lisbon when I was negotiating the Bosnian question, I saw -- he came to see me several times - he was very helpful - and he sent me documents from time to time that he thought might interest me. And I didn't -- did read -- I didn't send them back to him, did read the telegram in which that was clearly stated, an American telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you see any difference between the manner in which the Europeans viewed the Bosnian war and how it was viewed by the Americans?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: That is a vast question, Mr. Ivetic. How the Americans, all Americans, all -- how the Europeans, all the Europeans -- it's difficult to say. You see, among the Americans there was sometimes a tendency at that -- from politicians and from people who were not directly involved -- or who had not been directly involved with Yugoslavia to, as soon as they could, try to frame it in some kind of fight between good and evil. And the evil tended to fall on the Serbs in their view. People who have more -- Americans with more experience of Yugoslavia and I can think, for instance, of two that I knew very well. One fortunately still alive, it's Brent Scowcroft; the other was Larry Eagleburger. They both have been posted in different capacities in former Yugoslavia, and they knew that things were much more nuanced and that if you want -- also Americans, perhaps because of their history, tend to have sometimes - and again there are many expectations, I have just mentioned two that I came across - they tend to simplify little these problems. The Europeans have a long -- a long -- more than millennial history of internal fights of borders, of questions of dynasties. So we tend to have an in-built notion that things are not -- neither as easy nor as difficult as they look and that there are many shades of grey - if I may use the expression - when you look at the -- at an international problem of that kind. But this is just a kind of -- I mean, there is no -- I don't think there is "scientific" manner of distinguished between American views and European views. I mean, as I said, there are good views and bad views on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can look at paragraph 33 on the same page. It will be at the top of the page so we have to scroll up. And here you compare the Dayton Agreement with the Statement of Principles and lament the loss of countless lives which resulted after peace was not achieved in March 1992. Now you have touched on this already in answering some other questions. Do you have anything else you would like do add or comment further about this part of the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No, not really. I mean, the fact -- the big difference between what was arrived at at Dayton and then signed in Paris and what had been agreed in Sarajevo is that the Bosnian-Croat Federation or Muslim-Croat Federation was set. I don't see that necessarily as an improvement. But whatever it is, I mean, the -- the facts are that you still have a partition sought in the country but arrived at after a long and [indiscernible] and brutal war that didn't really help to create an a spirit of compromise. I think if the agreement had been reached, if the agreement reached before -- if -- was kept, if the parties had stuck with it, I don't know, could have evolved. The principles are principles and then there were lots of people that think that were to be discussed and you have just seen through the case of the working group on the -- on the establishment of the units, that it was not an easy job, neither for them nor for outsiders trying to help, in this case, the European Community. But if the outside pressure was kept from governments, we might have reached something very similar to Dayton earlier on and, as I said, with much less bad will created over the three and so years that passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 4, the prior page, of your statement in both copies.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to look at paragraph 26 with you. And here you talk about the killing on Vase Miskina Street. And in the very next paragraph, paragraph 27, you talk of the shelling of persons in a bread queue at Vase Miskina Street. How are these paragraphs related? Are these both relating to the same incident or are they two different incidents?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It's the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now in paragraph 27, you say a Portuguese army artillery officer involved in the investigation told you he was convinced the shell had come from the Bosnian government side. Can you provide us any more information as to the rank, position, or identity of this Portuguese army artillery officer who told you these things?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Firstly, he was not involved in the investigation. He was there as part of the European monitors. He was a artillery officer -- he is dead now. And he was there -- seen what other people saw, and he thought about it, and he knew what the positions were of the -- of the different parties. And he told me that he was convinced that it had been fired from the Muslim side and that -- and I had no reason to doubt his -- his -- his judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cutileiro, could I just try to make clear that earlier you corrected a mistake in -- about the letters. Here, do I understand you, that you stepping back from where, in paragraph 27, your statement reads: "He told me that he had participated in the investigation," that that is not an accurate portion of your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No, no, no. He had participated as a monitor as a European -- I don't think he was an investigator from the side of the Bosnian authorities. That was what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this has been clarified. And then could you explain a little bit further what, then, his role as a monitor was when investigations were ongoing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a monitor. There were -- the European Communities had monitors there, in -- for -- helping to keep the peace and so forth. And he -- he said that he had investigated the matter, but I don't think he was part of an official investigating team of the Bosnian government at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he was not technically equipped to deal with the scene where the shell had landed and to deal with all technicalities of what is usually investigated there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he went there, and he -- he had his own expertise, but I -- I don't know more about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we are at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's time for the break. Mr. Cutileiro, we will take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after the break. And I'll at this moment inquire with the parties. Mr. Ivetic, are we on track as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because -- and I'm now addressing both parties. We have a bit of a tight schedule whether we will be able to conclude hearing the testimony today. I think, as a matter of fact, we should try to do that and avoid that we need to come back tomorrow for ten or 15 minutes or for half an hour. If the parties could try to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can update. When I say I am on task, I actually mean to finish earlier than the hour and a half, so I should shave about 15 minutes off that time which might assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll take a break. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just like to verify whether the videolink is still functioning well. Could the representative of the Registry at the videolink location tell us whether he can see us and whether he can hear us -- hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we can see and hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the same is true in opposite direction. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a few more questions about this Portuguese army artillery officer that you told you about the Vase Miskina incident. When and where did you have occasion to speak with him on this topic, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I think it was in Sarajevo itself because I went to Sarajevo still a couple of times and I have known -- I have met him before, and that was it, yes. I -- I can't tell you precisely the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine. Do you recall what his rank was at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I think he was either a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel I think, but again ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you give us an idea of how you rated the reliability of this officer?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I -- I rate it very high. I -- he had impressed me as a very honest man. He was a Portuguese army officer with impeccable credentials. I mean, there is nothing -- he was not a pompous or [indiscernible] kind of person. He was a discreet, quiet man, and I have no reason to doubt what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, apart from this once incident at Vase Miskina, were there any other activities that you believed or that the -- that others in the UN communicated that were said to be the responsibility of the Bosnian government rather than the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: The case of the bread queue is the one that we have been talking was a very obvious case in which this officer that we have mentioned and other people were convinced that the thing had been presented as a Serb attack when it had not been so, the fact that there had been a television crew there and so forth. Other instances of similar magnitude I don't remember, and honestly, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And then what can you tell us about any observations - of yourself or others - in relation to the Bosnian government position as to the supplying of electricity and water to Sarajevo or the repair of utilities?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I don't recall at the moment anything specific. I think there were discussions about that, but I -- I didn't deal with that directly and I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you have any knowledge as to the implementation of safe areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, efforts to demilitarise them?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Safe areas came into being after I had stopped dealing with Bosnia, so I didn't hear anything directly then about it. I think this is right, because what I heard then -- because I still attended couple of meetings of the Vance-Owen Conference immediately in the beginning of 1993, but I -- I -- I don't -- as I said, I mean, safe areas were not part of our problem at the time. So what I heard, but again I have difficulty pinning down exactly who told me, is that often in safe areas people could come out at night and make war, if you wish, or attack peasants of -- in the case some of them Serbian peasants that lived nearby could be attacked or at least they thought they were attacked by people who were in the safe areas during the day and came back to that afterwards. But this, again, I couldn't pin it down to any specific conversation with anybody at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I thank you for your patience in answering my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have completed my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Cutileiro, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Tieger. You'll soon see him on your screen. Mr. Tieger is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, we would like to conclude your testimony today, so I would ask in that respect if you could keep your answers to questions I ask as focussed and responsive as possible with a yes or no, if it's possible, rather than expounding more generally on the subject matter raised. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. You refer in your statement in paragraph 28 to Dr. Karadzic's letter of 5 June 1992 which states in part that: "If you cannot keep your promises publicly announced by the EC, we have to protect Serbian people on their ethnic territories." Now your statement does not refer to your response to Dr. Karadzic, so I'd like to do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can the Registrar call up 65 ter 08886, and that would be behind tab 43 of the binder that Mr. Doraiswamy has. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we see here, you wrote back, among other things -- first you note in the last paragraph of your letter: "Let me add one thing referring to the last paragraph of your letter. The EC has not made any promises to you." And then you go on to explain that what happened instead was an agreement on a set of principles which can only be upheld on the basis of negotiated consensus and not force. So in that letter, you made a point of clarifying that what Dr. Karadzic had wrote you was not true and that, in fact, no promises had been made by the European Community; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It's written in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 08886 receives Exhibit Number P7767, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you discussed with Mr. Ivetic during your examination-in-chief paragraph 35 of your statement, referring in part to well-meaning outsiders and their view of the negotiations. Can we turn to tab 47 of the binder, and that's 65 ter 1D06136. You're probably seeing this ahead of the Judges, Ambassador, and so I'll say it's an article from the "New York Times" --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- titled: "US Policy Makers on Bosnia Admit Errors in Opposing Partition," and contains, among other things, the following excerpts. In the fourth paragraph down, Warren Zimmermann, then -- who was at -- who was contemporaneously, that is the time of the negotiations, American ambassador to Yugoslavia noting the following: "Our view was that we might be able to head off a Serbian power grab by internationalising the problem ... our hope was the Serbs would hold off if it was clear Bosnia had the recognition of western countries. It turned out we were wrong." And then if we look to the bottom of that first page, we see the point being made: "Other government specialists on Bosnia are skeptical that partition would have worked then" - and we turn the page - "or will work now without renewed fighting. If there was a flaw in United States policy, they say, it was more the failure to back up international recognition of an independent Bosnia with any meaningful support when Serbian and Croatian forces began shelling Muslim town centres and seizing territory through the terror tactics of ethnic cleansing." Ambassador, were aware of these alternate views about how to deal with the situation in Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: There were always alternative views of dealing. What I can tell you to cut time is that the model, if you wish, the principles that the team I led proposed and that were accepted were as it were at the time what -- what the market bore. I wouldn't have been able --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, excuse me, sir --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is perhaps a good opportunity to outline what I was mentioning before about responding. I'm not asking you to defend the negotiations that were taking place. Simply asking you if at the time you were aware of these alternative views of how to approach the problem?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I suppose I must have heard people saying that there were, but no proposal came to me in any way in that sense. And it's not, if I may, it's not only -- it's not defending my position. It is to tell you that the solution that was eventually found in Dayton is very, very close to what was being discussed three years before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, with respect you've offered that information in your statement, you repeated it again this morning. I'm trying to move quickly without inviting a repetition of the information already before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender this article, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D06136 receives Exhibit Number P7768, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, in your statement at paragraph 29, you make a point of noting that you received a letter from Dr. Karadzic that he was "firmly committed to stick to the principles of the agreement reached on the 18th of March, 1992."

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you, Mr. Ambassador, that Karadzic was only pretending to agree to the principles because he considered doing so tactically advantageous?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Anybody in the position in which I was would have to - from any of the parties - try to evaluate how seriously I could take it, but all parties sent their letters in the manner that they intended. We have been around Izetbegovic before this morning, but I -- I had no particular reason to believe that Dr. Karadzic wouldn't -- would be intent on not sticking to the principles of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me look at some of those principles and some of the things that Dr. Karadzic said to others, not necessarily to you, about those principles. One of the key, if not the key, aspect of the Statement of Principles was that Bosnia would be a state; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I heard you say "mm-hmm," in the affirmative. Or put another way, the --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It is affirmative in case you have a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Put another way the destruction of Bosnia was not considered to be part of the Statement of Principles; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up -- if we turn to tab 20 in the binder and call up P7023, e-court page 2, and in the Serbian page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a portion of a transcript of a session, the 49th Session, of the Republika Srpska Assembly held on the 13th of February, 1995. And at this portion of the session, Dr. Karadzic is speaking, and his remarks are reflected and he states the following: "The first position in all Cutileiro's principles, if you remember, was that Bosnia was a state consisting of this and that, but it always said that Bosnia was a state and we never accepted that, and we demanded the maximum that we could accept, Bosnia is a confederation of states, if we have to stay in some kind of a confederation. But our minimum is that our state is a state than it cannot can be drowned in anyone else's statehood and sovereignty except for the statehood and sovereignty of the Republic of Serbia, if we so wish, not even Yugoslavia because if it's Yugoslavia then we want to preserve our federal unit, our state, as a federative unit of this Federation, even though our priority was to become a part of Serbia." Can I take it, Ambassador, that Dr. Karadzic did not express this view to you during the course of negotiations --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Certainly not. Certainly not. It was, as you may -- again, I -- I can leave a bit yes or no question. The first position of the Serbs when I started was they didn't want an independent Bosnia. They didn't want Bosnia partitioned. They wanted to be part of Serbia. This he told me at the very beginning of the talks. But then, as we went on, they accepted the principles, which he as he himself says consisted in language of this and that, but it was a state and that -- that was it. This was held in February 1995 and our talks were in 1992. And Dayton, by the way, was in the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I think we're all aware of that those dates and we'll definitely keep then in mind. Now, the agreement in principle, for essentially the same reason, also did not envision or encompass the Bosnian Serb entity joining or uniting with Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So can we turn, please, to tab 11 of your binder and 65 ter 02345, e-court page 64 and Serbian page 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the 65 ter number and read it a little bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, this is a stenographic record of the 8th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People held in February 1992. And if you turn to, in that tab, about the fourth page you will see Mr. Krajisnik speaking. That's towards the bottom of the page in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're still not there in English on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's page 64 of the -- of e-court in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik states, speaking to the members of the assembly: "We have the opportunity to preserve the Serbian people in a single state, to preserve the entire Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and have it become part of the Serbian empire." And I take it, Ambassador, that this was not the position that Mr. Krajisnik or Dr. Karadzic asserted to you during the course of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Certainly not. Can I ask one thing? Mr. Krajisnik had some views that I sometimes thought particularly -- for instance, at a certain stage he thought that if they were going to have an agreement on the basis of the principles, then Bosnia should have three votes at the United Nations and three different flags; but Dr. Karadzic in that particular session told him to shut up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender this excerpt, Mr. President. Parts of this exhibit are already in evidence as P7005.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not clear as to what excerpts we're tendering. Are we just tendering the part that was read or the whole of the comments by Mr. Krajisnik in this part?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We can do either one, either that page or the whole of the comments if Mr. Ivetic wishes. I fully accept that I just referred to that page so I'm satisfied with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can deal with that then outside. We don't need to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the page or would you like later --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's do it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do the following. After a discussion by the parties, they'll inform the Chamber what 65 ter number should -- can be added to what is now in evidence as P7005. So we wait for the parties to agree on an excerpt. And, Madam Registrar, once we've received that, you'll be instructed to add that to P7005. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, similarly, if we could turn to tab 8 of the binder before you, Ambassador, and to 65 ter -- same 65 ter 02345, this time to e-court page 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that in English or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in ... yeah, and Serbian page 20, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And here we see at the same session Dr. Karadzic speaking and stating: "The aspirations of the Serbian people are" -- this is the bottom paragraph, please. "The aspirations of the Serbian people are very strong and the Serbian people will not rest until they have attained what they had during the time of the Nemanjic's their own state." And again, Ambassador, the same question: This was not the view expressed to you during the course of negotiations; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Certainly not. If it had been, we wouldn't have had agreement. This is done -- this session, if I -- is held on the 25th of February. The agreement is of the -- the -- my agreement is on 18th of March, so this was before. And, of course, on this basis I would not -- we would not have had agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd tender that excerpt under the same P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This excerpt to be added to what later then will be added to P7005. We'll wait for further agreement on the parties on this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, the agreement -- the -- the agreement in principles, the Statement of Principles was also not intended to be a trigger or signal to any of the parties to take control of or seize territory that they considered to be theirs or wanted to be theirs; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn then to tab 24 of the binder in front of you and to P4580, page 13, moving on to 14 in the English, and page 18 in the Serbian. Mr. Ambassador, this is a stenograph of the 11th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina that took place on the 18th of March, 1992, on the same date as the Statement of Principles. And involves, during the course of the discussion at that session, extensive focus on the negotiations and the Statement of Principles. Here, we see Mr. Krajisnik speaking and he states the following: "I think the problem is that they want Bosnia and Herzegovina to be internationally recognised at any cost. They want it to be a state. "In this respect it would be good if we could do one thing for strategic reasons, if we could start implementing what we have agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground. That we start determining the territory, and once the territory is determined, it remains to be established in additional negotiations whose authorities are to function" - turn the page in English - "and in what way. I cannot say whether this will be fair in political terms, there is not much fairness in politics after all, and yes, if it does not turn out to be fair, the Serbian people will be blamed. But we cannot accept a state designed in the mind of the SDA people." And I -- am I correct, Mr. Ambassador, that Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Karadzic did not tell you on the same day that the Statement of Principles was reached that they intended to begin implementing ethnic division on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd also like to look at -- all right. Mr. Ambassador, I asked you several questions about what Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik were telling you during the negotiations and positions they were taking in other contexts.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Dr. Karadzic spoke to you about being actually committed to the Statement of Principles because he considered that it had destroyed Bosnia and what remained was how much of Bosnia the certain entity would get? Did he tell you that during the course of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: The agreement had destroyed Bosnia; is that what you're asking me, if he asked me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he consider that that was the case and that was why he expressed his commitment to it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me that this agreement would finish Bosnia. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn next to tab 5 in your binder, and that would be P02391.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Tab -- excuse me, tab 5 is 65 ter 02391, e-court pages -- page 86 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's 65 ter not a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you, Your Honour. 65 ter 02391, yes. 02391, e-court page 86 in English and 70 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a tape-recording of the 39th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly held on the 24th and 25th of March, 1994, and again this is Dr. Karadzic speaking. And we see this in the middle of the page: "There was a Lisbon map too and the Muslims rejected it. We were happy when they rejected it. We accepted it in order to pull it into the Lisbon process. It was the wisdom and skill of Mr. Krajisnik, who pulled them into stating three things, into accepting three things - that there would be a division in three, that it would be based on ethnicity, and that there would be a referendum. We pulled them into it at that time when they said - we accept the division in three, and that it would be based on ethnicity. At that moment Bosnia was finished for the MZ - international community - that was a great achievement. The maps can be like this or like that. The maps can be widened even after ... signing." And again, Mr. Ambassador, did Mr. Karadzic tell you during the course of the negotiations that he considered that the Statement of Principles finished Bosnia for the international community?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I -- he never told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tendered this excerpt, Mr. President, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

If they had ignored us and kept quiet, recognised Bosnia, and said afterwards that there were some kind of insurrectionists there who were wrecking their own state, we would be in serious difficulties, nobody would be talking to us; by our pliability and willingness to negotiate we -- it seemed to them at every moment, there it is, except the Serbs have not agreed and that from the beginning right up until now, except that the Serbs -- I have not agreed -- not agreed and we led them on so that it seemed to them that they would be successful, that they would enter the process, that they would internationalise the Bosnian Question, because that very moment when Bosnia was internationalised ... Bosnia was finished and when they were recognised as a side in the conflict, although they say the government in Sarajevo and the government in Pale ..." utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, moving from the expression of this view by Dr. Karadzic, let me ask you this question: Were you aware of Dr. Karadzic's view that after Bosnia was "done" or "finished," the question was how much of it the Bosnian Serbs would get?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. I suppose once we had an agreement of principles, maps were going to be designed by the three parties with technical help, and eventually some bits will be found -- some borders would be found. So I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can put it more coherently in the context of a particular comment or two by Dr. Karadzic. So if I could turn your attention to tab 21 of the binder, and that's P4580, e-court pages 43 through 44 in English and 63 through 64 in Serbian and that would be, in Serbian, beginning around the second sentence of the fourth full paragraph. Now, once again, this is Dr. Karadzic speaking at the assembly session which was held on the 18th of March, 1992, the same day as the Statement of Principles, and at page 43 of the English, toward -- in the last paragraph, Dr. Karadzic states the following: "We have preserved the Serbian people as a corpus, in its entirety, in the BH and detached it as an entity, and now it is a matter of quantity only. We have achieved the quality. This is what Europe recognises: Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina exists. The only remaining question is the one of quantity, there is a tug of war about who will have more. We won, we have drawn the rope to a certain point and we are not going to yield it back. There is no return to a unitary BH, we can go forward and obtain more power for the constituent units. So, we have led them into the waters, into which we wanted to lead them. The fact that it is not up to here (showing at his neck) but only to the waist, that has to do with quantity." And if we turn the page in English, he continues -- and Serbian as well, please. It continues: "And it will happen according to our political will, our right to self-determination and organisation, it will happen according to the actual conditions which are up to you to create." Now, Ambassador, you already alluded to the difficult questions of defining the territories of the constituent units indicated in the Statement of Principles. Did Dr. Karadzic emphasise to you during the course of the negotiations his view that Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina exists, now the only remaining question was how -- was one of quantity, how big it was going to be, and that he was emphasising to his followers that it would be up to the actual conditions which were to them to create?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Is that -- is that the information Dr. Karadzic was emphasising to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: We had come to an agreement and then each party had then to convince their own people. He didn't go into details like that to me. He went back to his people and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. One more excerpt before we take a recess, and that's at tab 27 of your binder, sir, and 65 ter 02345, e-court page 20 in English and page 24 in Serbian.

utterances.text: This is Dr. Karadzic speaking at one of the sessions I referred your attention to earlier, Ambassador, the 8th Session held on the 25th of February, 1992, and these are the words he spoke at the assembly: "We accept, and I say BH must remain within these borders. Great. Now let us turn to internal borders. And once that is done, once they are wider than the external borders, then we can say, who cares about external borders. What matters is that the ones within BH become as wide as possible. As the popular saying goes, if kicked out the door, go back through the window. You will still be in the same place." During the course of the negotiations, was Dr. Karadzic emphasising to you his intention to ensure that the borders were as wide as possible?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that we can start thinking about what to do in our leisure time, isn't it, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.text: Well, I was going to suggest that, but I was leaving that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, just before we recessed we had been looking at the question of quantity and wide borders. In that connection, I wanted to ask you if Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik during the course of negotiations emphasised certain factors that I'm going to bring to your attention that -- that implicated the extent of the borders. So this Court has received evidence, for example - that's P3006 for benefit of the Court and parties - the declaration of the proclamation of the state, that the territories of the Bosnian Serb republic were considered to include areas in which the Serbian people is now a minority due to the genocide carried out against it in World War II. And we also see that in P3007, Article 2, of the Constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, that the territory was considered to include regions where genocide was committed against the Serb people in the Second World War. Did Mr. Karadzic emphasise to you or indicate to you during the course of negotiations that he considered that the Bosnian Serb entity should include territories on which the Bosnian Serb people were a minority?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Not that I remember. But I don't exclude it. You know, we discussed the principles, and then we were going and we did go for a while on the maps, and the basic -- the basis for working on the maps was the current - at the time - the demographic reality. And there was no absolutely recent census, if I remember rightly, but it was on the last available census. And the kind of - if I may comment - mythical, historical notion of territories that had once been people populated by one of the -- one of the groups, and that for one reason or another in the war perhaps, would have stopped being -- that group would have stopped being a majority. I don't think we would accept that. I know we didn't accept that as an argument. So at the time when we came to discuss maps, that was not an issue anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in connection with the mention of the mythical nature of that view of territorial entitlement, let me just turn briefly to tab 46 of your binder, 65 ter 02366, e-court page 32 and Serbian page 23. This is a tape-recording of the 24th Session of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska held on the 8th of January, 1993. And this is a delegate from Prijedor in north-west Bosnia speaking, Mr. Srdic. And he says: "Also from this place I want to say that I was shocked with the map presented to us by our respected President, Mr. Karadzic. What do those renegades think, that we have spilled our blood and conquered what belongs to us all for nothing? We have conquered -- actually restored only the Serb territory that they took from us back in 1941 when they conducted a massacre over the Serb people. Gentlemen, and I can tell you only this, and I believe that I share the opinion of the neighbouring municipalities of Bosanska Novi, Bosanska Krupa, and Sanski Most not a single inch of the land shall be given to those vile traitors and brats who want to share the municipality of Prijedor as well as other municipalities the way it suits them. It is the greeting from under Kozara. We will fight until the very last man" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "That is the greeting from under Kozara. We will fight until the very last man and not a single inch of land shall we give." Now, Ambassador, we'll look reasonably soon at, for example, the maps that you referred to, the Dayton map, and what happened during the course of the conflict, but I simply wanted to draw your attention to this and ask if you were aware of the time -- I'd already asked you, of course, about the provisions in the declaration, the proclamation of the state, and in the constitution, if you were aware of the fact that those historical or mythical views of entitlement to territory were reflected in not only the legal documents but in exchanges of views at the Parliament in positions taken by the representatives of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Again, I -- I have difficulty with your question. Obviously these are difficult questions and they are difficult questions particularly in a place where history is of extreme importance - it is much more important than law in many cases - for what people feel. But, as you know, I was not a member of the People's Assembly of the Republika Srpska, and in January 1993 I didn't deal with Bosnia anymore. So I'm sure this is what happened, and I'm sure many other people had these kind of views. But when they were negotiating map, the bits that we did on that, obviously this was not an argument that we could accept, so probably that's why Karadzic was -- if I understand well the quotation, what you have just showed, the Serbs negotiators had difficulties with their own assembly. But that's part of a deal like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that excerpt, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the excerpt as such is uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it should be added to P6921 -- no, it is not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the excerpt will be under uploaded and will then be added and Madam Registrar will be instructed to add it to P6921. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to look at another basis or motive that implicated the extent of the borders and claim territory, and in that respect wanted to turn your attention to tab 26 in your binder, which is P4584, e-court pages 5 through 6 and Serbian pages 6 through 7. This is Dr. Karadzic speaking at a session of the 53rd Assembly, Republika Srpska National Assembly, in 1995, talking about what has happened and why. And he says at the bottom of the page in English and toward the bottom quarter of the page on page 7 in the Serbian: "To tell the truth, there are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves" - and now next page in English - "and there were only 30 per cent of us" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not yet on our screens. Could you wait for a second. It's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it there also in -- apparently not in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the bottom of the page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The very bottom, I think. Yes. And now in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next page in B/C/S, please. And enlarge the bottom quarter of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Dr. Karadzic states: "To tell the truth, there are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In English, not in B/C/S, please.
