utterances.text: Could we then go back in B/C/S. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance they had to become ours, and no one is practically questioning it anymore." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger when was this session held?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1993 and specifically 28th of August -- 1995, excuse me, and specifically 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask you to remember those or keep those specific areas named in mind, because I'll be directing your attention to them in connection with a later document as well. But I simply wanted to ask you whether during the time of negotiations, as you were considering the prospect of negotiating on territory, whether Dr. Karadzic emphasised that there were strategic reasons which dictated that the Bosnian Serbs should obtain multiple areas where the Bosnian Muslims were, in fact, a majority?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, Ambassador, even setting aside for a moment these factors which implicated the extent of the territory that the Bosnian Serb leadership considered should be Serbian, the international negotiators understood that the maps did not speak favourably about ethnic division; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I can't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be clearer if I turn your attention to a specific portion of notes taken during the course of those discussions, and in that connection if I could turn your attention to tab 10 of your document, and this is 65 ter 0958.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I hope these look familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that one digit is missing which would enable to find that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, 07958 and I obviously must have omitted one of those digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I was just saying that I hope these look familiar to you. You had an opportunity to review them when Mr. Hayden and I met with you in, I believe, 2009 --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- and you indicated at that time that they appeared to accurately reflect what had taken place during the course of the negotiations, although obviously you were unable to conduct an extensive exhaustive review. I think you said the following. You were able to verify the document to the extent that the dates recorded reflect the actual dates of the talks and that it does appear to be a genuine attempt to recreate what happened. "The topics discussed are consistent with my recollection of the matters raised by Mr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serbs in these separate talks." Is that still consistent with your understanding of that document?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I point out to that you that that document is of the 6th of February, 1992, which was my first visit to Sarajevo - I accompanied Lord Carrington. And it was at that meeting that Lord Carrington told the Bosnians in general - Izetbegovic, Karadzic, and the representatives of the Croats as well - that we were going to have a set of negotiations to try to get a political solution for Bosnia. And these were the negotiations I chaired. So this is previous to that. We started our talks couple of weeks later, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: -- and so this is not exactly -- well, it is a -- I was there. It is a conversation between Lord Carrington and Dr. Karadzic, and, yes, they said what is said is there. But this is at -- we have not yet even started --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I understand that, Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: -- negotiating the Bosnian question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before we continue, I see at this moment in the original a cover -- cover of what seems to be a kind of a booklet. But in the English translation, there is some comment on the top three lines of comment what it may be and to whom it belongs, et cetera, which I do not see in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I think that's why -- it should be in brackets, I imagine. That's how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even I expect a translation to just translate what is in the original document and not any -- with or without brackets any further comments to what it claims to present. Therefore, if you later want to tender part of this, I think that the comment should be removed from what is now presented as an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm happy to do so, Mr. President. I would indicate that it's significant for provenance purposes that this document was tendered by Dr. Karadzic as the notes taken by his chef de cabinet relating to the negotiations Ambassador Cutileiro --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We might be very much interested to know what it says, but it should not be part of the translation where in the original it doesn't say anything about that. That's my only comment at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. No, we'll take care of that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I wanted to bring your attention to two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I note that the B/C/S translation isn't coming through. Perhaps the microphones are not turned on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- do you now receive B/C/S translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need to repeat what was just said, which was just a technical issue of -- in the translation appearing some text what does not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- not needed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll move on. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention, Mr. Ambassador, to two portions of that. The first one is contained at page 3 of the document and it's during the course of that meeting involving -- that's headed "Lord Carrington visiting Dr. Karadzic." And there Lord Carrington is recorded as stating: "The map of BiH" - and this is in the middle of the page - "is not speaking in favour of division of Bosnia." This was a reflection, was it not, Mr. Ambassador, of the fact that the question of the division of Bosnia was already on the table and Lord Carrington's position that the map of Bosnia - meaning the demographics of Bosnia - did not speak favourably about the prospect of that division?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Well, this is what is written here, so he certainly said that. And there are probably parts of the world where maps would reflect more -- would speak differently in favour or disfavour of a division, but this was one possibility; there were others. And in the end what we managed to get agreement on from Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, was the division on the three constituent units. I don't want to take time - because I only want to finish early, if possible - but the Muslims didn't want any division at all. The Serbs didn't want Bosnia do exist. They wanted to -- things being carved in a way that the Serbs would remain in Serbia and this is a particular extreme case of elasticity of borders, if you wish. The Croats were more discreet in what they wanted, but basically they would have profited if Bosnia disappeared and Serbs would remain in Serbia and the Croats -- particularly the Croats of Herzegovina would have gone to Croatia. What eventually we arrived at where they all were still talking to each other, the coalition government was in place, which was the tripartite thing which - if I may remember - with the addition of the Muslim-Croat Federation is what you find in Dayton. I'm saying this because obviously on the onset looking -- without looking or discussing with -- with the people concerned, you might have imagined different ways of trying to sort out the Bosnian question, but that was the way that in the end we managed to get agreed upon by the parties themselves. So the comment of Lord Carrington is absolutely normal and it's there. That's what it said. But this is -- again, this is before we had tried to probe the question with the three constituent -- the three parties, the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. For the moment I'm focussing on the issue of division and the extent of the territory claimed. Let me move to a portion of this record of the negotiations deeper into the negotiations, in particular, on the 27th of February - that's page 8 - where the same issue appears to be raised. And we can look at the bottom of the page. We see Dr. Karadzic saying: "Essentially they are taking us out of Yugoslav forever and are closing us into BiH." Mr. Koljevic speaks: "Are Muslims going to accept ethnic principles?" And then it says: "Darvin" - I presume that's a reference to Henry Darwin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It says -- it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "-- states: "'I cannot accept that they become ethnically clean entities because it is not feasible in the field." That's another reflection, is it not, Mr. Ambassador, of the view that the demographic distribution in Bosnia did not speak favourably of the possibility of ethnic division?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It depends on how you did it, you see, because you -- the -- what we call loosely the international community - and that means in this case basically Europe and the United States - wanted an independent Bosnia. And the three people that were the main people there found no better way to sort that out and to get an independent Bosnia than by having three constituent units with appropriate protection for minorities and so forth. This was the case in 1992 and this was the case in -- since then, until 1995. It was with us all the time. There were attempts by Owen and Vance and then by Owen and Stoltenberg that they wished to negotiate different arrangements. That didn't work. And eventually when Dick Holbrooke took over, we went back basically to the original arrangement. Neither of this is satisfactory, but it was what was possible. It was what was the market bore as I said. We were aware from the beginning of these difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender those excerpts, Mr. President, and I don't believe there is an existing number yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently no objection. Could the Chamber be informed about the -- I do understand, Mr. Tieger, that it was tendered in the Karadzic case by Mr. Karadzic and it is presented as being a notebook of Mr. Karadzic's secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: His chef de cabinet, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Chef de cabinet, yes. If there's no dispute about that on the origin of this. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 07958 receives Exhibit Number P7770.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admission is complete, but we expect the English version to be -- that the comment will be taken out of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, we've looked at a number of concepts or positions that implicated the extent of the territory claimed and the potential position on the map appended to the Statement of Principles which, as I believe you've indicated, was a map that reflected the existing demographic distribution in Bosnia by municipalities. I'd like to look next in that regard at Exhibit P7294. The transcript is at pages 1 to 2 of the English and the Serbian, but I'd like to look -- this is a video recording of Dr. Karadzic speaking about the map, and I'd like to play that for your benefit and for the benefit of the Court and parties, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the audio been reviewed against the excerpt --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- this is -- yes, it's already in evidence and it's already been reviewed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not receive English translation. Have the transcript been distributed to the booth? They have. Could we re-start and are the interpreters -- do they know -- I see there is a bit of gesturing between the various booths.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are trying to locate the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you inform us one you've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We just provided one this morning and there's a note on it that identifies it as beings this document in connection with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have a copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A copy is there. I see everyone is smiling so we could continue. Could we re-start, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Mr. President, ever since the Lisbon Conference took place, we entered a real epic of maps. World politics didn't operate with maps so much until then. Please explain to our public, the Serbian public, certain issues that remained unexplained all this time. Shall we start? What was happening after the Cutileiro Plan? "Radovan Karadzic: You're right. The fact that the main problem has always been the map tells us that this map -- this war was about territory. Here before us is the Cutileiro preliminary map which had recognised around 50 per cent of our territory before the war had even started and before any kind of so-called aggression had occurred which was not entirety satisfactory to us but we accepted the logic of the map and that's why we accepted it because for the first time it was about the separation of Bosnia into three pieces. You see, for instance, remember this, it will be very important to us later as regards the western part, they accepted the border to be at the Una River. They acknowledged that there were Muslims at the foothills of Mount Grmec and Mount Kozara, but they expected that we would trade it for something like they expected us to trade something in the area of Mount Kupres, part of Mount Kupres for Posavina. However, this map here shows something that all the future maps would show, which is the necessity of cutting off the Serbian territory at Brcko. The western interests are making sure that the Serbian state is not established, that -- "Journalist: Therefore, it is a rope around the neck from the beginning of the Serbs in the long run? "Radovan Karadzic: Yes, absolutely. We didn't want to accept the map but we decide it was a major step forward because the Muslims thought we wouldn't accept it. We ensured that it would be written 'preliminary' on it and then we accepted it and it was the first time that the Muslims and Croats accepted to divide Bosnia into three pieces. We weren't satisfied with an Eastern Bosnia, with Sarajevo too, although we can see that Sarajevo is divided between the Serbs and Muslims. We weren't satisfied with the Neretva River valley, especially not here. We were satisfied here with the Una River and we could accept that. Look at this map here which is in fact the Vance-Owen Plan which shows the black fields represent what we would have to give back if we had accepted the Vance-Owen Plan. You see, once again, you can notice that we're cut off here at Brcko. "Journalist: For the exit too? "Radovan Karadzic: Yes, but not only at Brcko. In this scenario we would have lost Mount Ozren, Doboj, and entire Posavina, and then a large area in the Eastern Bosnia and here, of course, is Western Bosnia. You see, we saw on Vance's table special maps of mineral resources and other resources which were issued by the Central Investigations Agency, the CIA, and there we saw that a lot of attention given to the Ljubija mining facility, the Kamengrad coal-mine, and all the central mines here and the power plants on the Drina River and the Neretva River. Therefore, the west has always been making sure that it be given to Croats, and I must say that all the Croats have a true friend which is Germany. Neither are the Americans friends of the Muslims nor have the Russians done anything for us, whereas the Croats would always only accept that was offered as Germany already made sure that they'd got the right thing. "Journalist: You've mentioned Ljubija. It's interesting that Goerring had exploited that same area during the Second World War. I believe that the CIA had taken most of these resource maps from the Germans. That's the essence of it in my opinion. "Radovan Karadzic: In that regard you can understand why a green -- a green stain has appeared here. Another German -- actually an Austrian Valdheim had carried out genocide here. Here, for instance, in Sanski Most over 5.300 Serbs were killed, murdered, and slaughtered in one day. In this area here in Bosanska Krupa even and Bihac, the Bihac county, we were absolutely the majority of the population in this area, more than two-thirds. Somewhere between 70 per cent and 77 per cent of the population were Serbs. And now when you tell someone from the foothills of Mount Grmec and Mount Kozara that a part of Mount Kozara, a part of Mount Grmec, the Sana River valley, et cetera, which have always been exclusively Serbian, for the most part Serbian, that it will become someone else's, you can expect a negative response, not just from the people here but from all the people here as well who will not allow that to happen to the Serbs here. A complete national solidarity and self-awareness is present here and everybody equally worries about how the state will be."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you've just had an opportunity to see along with the rest of us Dr. Karadzic speaking about the map and indicating his dissatisfaction with the map in respect of Eastern Bosnia, Sarajevo, the Neretva, the "green stain" in north-west Bosnia. Did Dr. Karadzic express to you his dissatisfaction with these significant portions of the Cutileiro map during the course of your negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I suppose you call the Cutileiro map the original map, which was a basis for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies, I made the same -- I did the same thing to Mr. Ivetic was referring to earlier. The map appended to the Statement of Principles.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Well, the map was a basis to start discussions, and discussions were started. And all parties had their arguments in one way or another, but nothing of the kind that I have just heard was told to me in that way. This is certainly not a thing that appeared. We knew it was difficult - you yourself said why it was difficult - and we were doing as we could. But you -- the maps that was -- that were finally agreed were the maps that were agreed in Dayton, so you probably should ask the people who were in Dayton whether this kind of arguments or reservations lasted there. I don't remember that being so important because at my time we didn't come to a detailed overall map of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the three constituent units. We were in the preliminary phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, Mr. Ambassador, as you yourself have written, once recognition -- once Bosnia was recognised as independent or recognition was imminent and the negotiations from the Bosnian Serb point of view unsuccessful, the Bosnian Serbs felt confirmed in their paranoid view of history and went brutally on the offensive; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I wrote that in an article, but I don't -- at the stage in which I was talking to you, which is the stage of the preliminary map with the principles, I don't think you can take that map as an example because further maps were negotiated later, particularly in the Dayton process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going look at what those maps were based in part on. But first if we could quickly turn to tab 42 of the binder in front of you, page 40 of the documents listed there, and it's 65 ter 1D04315 -- [Microphone not activated] if we could enlarge the last paragraph on the left column, please. That's the article to which you were referring, Mr. Ambassador - is that correct? - where you wrote: "Recognition triggered the war. The Serbs felt confirmed in their paranoid view of history and went brutally on the offensive"?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Mr. Tieger, we don't have the right document. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's page 40 of the documents in tab 42, and they're paginated on the bottom of the page in pencil, I believe. It should be the second-to-last document in that -- under that tab.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it a manuscript document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ambassador, it's a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, then it's something.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'm afraid we have the wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you see tab 42? It should have about 40 pages of documents under it, and the second-to-last page is a copy of this newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it in front of me, yes. Yes? Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender that. If -- just the one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D04315 receives Exhibit Number P7771, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, were you aware before these offensive operations began that the Bosnian Serb leadership had contemplated doing so even as the negotiations were in progress or before the agreement in principle was reached?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: We hoped that it would not happen. I didn't know of any Serbian plans. Recognition was necessary to put Bosnia in the map of international relations and we had expected that the three parties would go on negotiating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to a few documents, if I may. First document behind tab 8 of your binder, 65 ter 02345, e-court page 21, page 25 in the Serbian, the bottom one-third of the page. And in your binder, Mr. Ambassador, it should be about the --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- fifth page in there marked page 21 of that --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But hard copy -- no, it's the fifth page but paginated as 21 on the --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: 21, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And there it's Mr. Krajisnik speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he says the following: "As I was a participant in the Lisbon talks I would like to add a few remarks" -- and I should draw your attention to the fact that this is the 8th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People held on the 25th of February, 1992. "As I was a participant in the Lisbon talks, I would like to add a few remarks," Mr. Krajisnik says. "Today we must discuss the first item which is crucial for the Serbian people. Gentlemen, we have two options: One to fight by political means to make the most out of the present time, as a first phase; or to break off the talks and go for what we have done over the centuries: Win our own territories by force." And then later, if we turn to the very next page, and page 64 in the e-court in English and page 81 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Um, in the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Same document. Just turn the page and I'm directing your attention to the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I'm on page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, and if you turn the page you will see -- these are excerpts. You turn that page, it should be paginated page 64.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I haven't got it --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's the last page in the tab, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read it out because it's just one sentence --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- with the indulgence of my colleagues. Again, it's page 64 in the English and page 81 in the Serbian. Mr. Krajisnik says -- it's actually two -- two or three sentences: "Gentlemen, we want to remain in a single state together with Serbia, Montenegro, the Independent Autonomous Region of Krajina, now the Krajina state, and the rest, we just need to agree on the method to achieve this. "If we don't want to do this by certainly methods, let us put a stop to it. You know what our profession has always been - to wage war."

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Karadzic during the course of negotiations emphasising to you that if -- that they were contemplating if the results of the negotiations were not sufficiently satisfactory to simply win their territories by force?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No, to me they didn't say that. They were trying to keep negotiating. They liked, in fact, to show that they -- or they said that they were keen to negotiate and that -- and I'm quoting them as I remember, it was the Muslims who didn't want to go on negotiating. They did want to go on negotiating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those excerpts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember. But again, I mean, I was not in the Serbian Republic Assembly and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it should be added to P7005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This portion still to be uploaded and the 65 ter number to be -- to be given then will be added to P7005.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I direct your attention, Ambassador, to remarks by Mr. Krajisnik. Let me also direct your attention to remarks by Dr. Karadzic behind tab 5 of your binder, and that's 65 ter 2391?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, Mr. Tieger, may I just draw to your attention to part of the previous exhibit, which was the notebook of the chef de cabinet of Mr. Karadzic. I think you dealt with one page and in e-court it was 64 pages. Could you --

utterances.text: Yeah, and I think -- first of all, I think I dealt with two pages --

utterances.text: Could you again give the details of the document you are calling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is now P7769.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, not the entirety, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this would be page 88 of the English and page 72 of the Serbian beginning about the tenth line down from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a tape-recording of the 39th Session of the RS National Assembly - we referred to that before - and again Dr. Karadzic is speaking. And he says the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the middle -- almost smack in the middle of the page, Your Honour. If you look at -- I'm trying to think of something -- there is the designation [sic] after the end of one sentence in the middle of the page, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then this is where -- and the passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.text: There are two "sics."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this is the one in the middle of the page I think and it begins -- the portion I'm going to read is "before the war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where can we find it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: About ten lines down from the top of the page -- or from the bottom of the page, excuse me. No, no, no. That's -- I was correct the first time. So about ten lines down from the top of the page, and it starts toward the right-hand part of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I see the name Milojevic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the -- Milojevic is at approximately eight lines down from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is Dr. Karadzic speaking: "Before the war, Professor Milojevic while anticipating whatever would happen with that BiH, we were making plans and it turned out to be almost similar to what will be in Sarajevo. We were thinking then to capture Zvijezda Mountain and that it would be the border. The canyon of the Krivaja River would serve then for connecting Sarajevo and Banja Luka, so that the distance between Sarajevo and Banja Luka could be covered, on a good road, in 1.5. That is a state. That is a well-integrated nation. That was our plan way back before the war." And again, Mr. Ambassador, did Dr. Karadzic relate to you during the course of negotiations that his plans even before the negotiations were taking place and he -- included capturing certain parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina territory?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender that and ask that it be added to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The excerpt still to be uploaded under a 65 ter number still to be announced will then be added to P7769. Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Moving to a slightly different topic and which will involve looking at a number of maps, so probably best to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then apparently your optimism has not become a reality in one session, but how much would we still need after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will certainly conclude in the next session, Mr. President, unless something completely unforeseen happens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the next session. Then Mr. Ivetic would still need time for -- I think you announced that you're still optimistic to finish in this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's another case of no good deed going -- I would be seen as having made appropriate progress if I hadn't been over-optimistic. We moved at a slower pace than the first session. I'm still moving as quickly as possible and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- will try to complete as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you try to see whether you could find, together with Mr. Ivetic, perhaps I have no idea how much time he would need in re-examination, how -- how we could achieve to finish still today even if there would be a small extended session perhaps. And I ask Madam Registrar whether there's any option to -- well, to go on for, let's say, 15 minutes -- or 15 to 20 minutes, if that would be agreeable to the Defence, because if Mr. Mladic would insist on finishing on quarter past 2.00, we would do so. Could all parties try to see whether we can achieve that. We'd like to take a break, Mr. Cutileiro. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. We'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the parties reached an understanding on how to finish today or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, not quite in that sense, but I've reduced my areas to three. I hope I can move through quickly. I projected a completion time for Mr. Ivetic that should allow him sufficient time according to him so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because there's one decision that the Chamber would like to deliver today, but that takes another four to five minutes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I'll try to move quickly. At paragraph 32 of your statement tendered to the Court, you indicated that Dr. Karadzic expressed his willingness to return territory to the Muslims. Now, this Trial Chamber has received in evidence, among other things, a -- notes from a meeting between Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic in August of 1992 - that's P354, page 22 in English and 29 in Serbian - during which Dr. Karadzic said to General Mladic: "The European community will accept the factual situation which is why we must not make any concessions militarily." And I also wanted to bring to your attention and ask you a question about that. That's -- this is something found at tab 33 of your binder. It's P7357, page 5 of the English, pages 4 and 5 in Serbian, beginning on the fourth line from the bottom on page 4 in Serbian. And the portion in English starts on the third line above the number 29 in the middle of the page: "Our goal is to create a state. How big it will be, we do not know, but it has to be in one piece. And in order for the state to exist, it has to be in one piece. We have to maintain this reality as long as the world accepts this idea. "We have created new realities. Speaking in narrow terms, Zvornik used to be 60:40 to the advantage of Muslims, but the Serbs from Zenica came, they occupied Kozluk, the Muslims left for Europe and I do not know where else. And those gentlemen told us - who gives you the right to ask for Zvornik? We said that the whole Bosnia was the Serbian land. That is the history, but it is not what we are interested in. Who gives you a right to request Zvornik now? We request Zvornik based on the right which comes out of a new reality. This war had created the new reality. It has never happened in history that the war did not create a new history. This war has created the new reality: There are now the Serbs from Zenica here. If you want to give Zvornik to the Muslims then you have to wage a new war in order to expel these Serbs back to Zenica. We request Zvornik according to this right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you just give the date of this session for the witness because I think you didn't do that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't do that. It's 1994, the 9th -- I think it's contained in his binder, the 9th through 11th November and 23rd November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So when Dr. Karadzic indicated to you, as you indicated in your statement, that his willingness to return territory, did he also indicate his view of creating new realities and the effect of a fait accompli on which territories he would be willing to return?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Next I'd like to draw a couple of excerpts to your attention. That's -- first one is found at tab 39 of your binder. It's 65 ter 02388 at pages 126 through 127; and Serbian page 94, the third full paragraph. This is a session of the 37th Assembly Session held on 10th of January, 1994. The first speaker we see is Mr. Maksimovic, president of the Deputies Club, and at the bottom paragraph on page 126, he states: "What I would really like to see here, is a firm attitude" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is quite difficult to follow. We -- I don't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we blow up, the last paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "What I would really like to see here is a firm attitude that the Muslims and the Croats will not be allowed to return to the areas under our rule. Accordingly, we should not return to the areas that will be under the Croatian rule. I think that we should be decisive about this. Otherwise, I am afraid that those people from Sandzak will occupy Srbinje and surrounding areas because there are too many of them in that area."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we missed the link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the videolink apparently is -- should be re-established.

utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I think we're okay from our end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we still cannot see you. We can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh. I have the paper in front of me that I was following what Mr. Tieger was reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still do not have the video. We hear what is said at the videolink location but cannot see you yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for a message whether it can be resolved soon or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are we on the right page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that finished our chances to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we still give it a try, Mr. -- I think that we see you now again. If Mr. Registrar would say a few words, we can confirm that we hear him and perhaps the confirmation would be that he sees us and hears us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, confirmed on both accounts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would be page 94 of the Serbian, please, and it's the document that -- with ERN 02152154. That's it. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We had ended, referring to Mr. Maksimovic's remarks, he continues at the bottom of the page in English: "So we should take a firm position and ban any ... returns to the territories we have gained through these international combinations" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn the page. Now we're on page 126 the B/C/S -- of the English in e-court. Okay. That's it. And he continues on. I think we can see that and the witness has had a chance to see it: "I do not care if the Muslims will live at all, where they will live, whether they will have a country or not. I am not interested in that. The only thing I'm interested in is my people and the territory where my people live. Therefore, any thought about having 500 or more Muslims within our future country is out of the question." And then at page 132 of the English and 98 in the Serbian Dr. Karadzic responds: "As to the return of the refugees, I owe an answer to Vojo's question" - that's Vojislav Maksimovic - "according to the international law, we have no right to ban the return of the refugees. In principle, all refugees can return, but I would just add one sentence: This also has to be a two-way process. "The Muslims and the Croats accepted the two-way process. Later on Owen asked me: Why did you insist on the two-way process? But when the Serbs from Zvornik returned to Zenica, then the Muslims from Prijedor will return to Prijedor. Therefore, it must be a two-way process. In accordance with the international law, we cannot declare a ban of the return of refugees."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in a same vein, Mr. Ambassador, if you could turn to tab 40, the very next tab, the same issue is raised at 65 ter 02418.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And of course I'll be tendering these excerpts, Mr. President, but in the interests of time I think we can handle that -- this previous one will be added to P3076. Now in 65 ter 02418, if we could turn to page 29 of the English and the bottom page 36 in Serbian; 65 ter 02418, page 29 in English. Okay. We see at item 5, and that's what we're looking for, the portion marked number 5, this is Dr. Karadzic speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it in B/C/S, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's page 36 in B/C/S at the bottom, moving on to page 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There, it's at the bottom there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Full catalogue of human rights and inserted: Freedoms as listed in international instruments, et cetera, including the right of refugees and displaced persons to be able to return, we have now added which must be an overall process. They don't know what that is, so they kept shifting the first part of the sentence. That's our intention, to say, all right, everyone has the right to return to his home after the war, if that is an overall process. What does that mean, an overall process? That means that the Muslims from Kozluk can return to Kozluk, if the Serbs from Kozluk return to Zenica. If they don't want to return, then we need, and if they cannot return, then we need a new war to exchange that, and that's why I think we should always insist on this. So an overall process, either overall or none at all. "We can act the Serbian Cyrillic way and tell it all to their face, or we can be a bit cunning, we do have to be a bit cunning." Mr. Ambassador, did Dr. Karadzic tell you that you was attempting to implement cunning approaches to ensure that the de facto situation that had been created in, for example, Kozluk, would remain as it was?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Certainly not. But as you have noticed, this document is from 1995, it's from after Dayton. In the -- or about that time. No, to me, he didn't tell anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender those excerpts, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Added to P4584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you have not yet uploaded the excerpt; that will be done, we'll be informed about the 65 ter number, and we'll then instruct Madam Registrar to add it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Ambassador, you referred during the course of your testimony today and in paragraph 33 of your statement to the Dayton Accords and indicated that a comparison of the map, the Dayton map, to the map annexed to the Statement of Principles, indicated that the result was about the same. And I wanted to look very quickly at the two maps which we can find at tab 29 of the binder and at 65 ter 17597. Ambassador, that's about this coloured representation of the Dayton map was confirmed by you in the Karadzic case and reflects with a visual depiction rather than the hash marks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it says the Cutileiro Plan March 1992 what we see on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Ambassador, the green-red-and-blue map marked Cutileiro Plan, March 1992, and behind is it the Dayton map. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the witness is nodding yes. Apparently he sees it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that we could have the two --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Side by side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- side by side on our screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The ERN -- the 65 ter for the Dayton map is 17982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Still the same map here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not very helpful -- well, perhaps we get --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, looking at it quickly, the areas in green reflect Muslim areas in the case of the Cutileiro Plan map, Muslim-majority areas at the time; and in the Dayton map, we see that the Muslim-Croat Federation areas are depicted in pink and the Serb areas in orange. So looking quickly at Eastern Bosnia, we see that the swaths of green reflected by the Muslim-majority areas there have given way to an almost -- total area of orange which are the Serb areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I'm looking at the maps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So areas that were once Muslim-majority areas were now -- now became part of the Serb entity; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: In which map?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Areas that were Muslim-majority areas as depicted in the Cutileiro Plan map of March 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- are now part of the Serb area under the Dayton Accords; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking more closely at those areas in the Cutileiro map and referring back to Dr. Karadzic's remarks at the 53rd Session regarding the areas of strategic importance that had to be Serb, he referred to Bratunac, Srebrenica, Visegrad, Rogatica, Vlasenica, and Zvornik. And those are all municipalities which were Muslim-majority areas in 1992 and which became part of the Serb entity under the Dayton Accords; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was -- that was because the Muslim -- or that reflected at least the fact that the majority Muslim population in those areas were no longer there; right? That they had been displaced.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Possibly. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that, Ambassador, reflected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- yes, I think there was a bit of a problem with overlapping speakers but I heard you say "possibly." That's... what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thanks. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, that was a difference between the two maps which reflected the destruction of hundreds of communities, the displacement of tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of people and the deaths of many thousands, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It's very difficult to compare what you call the Cutileiro Plan map, which was a preliminary plan, that was attached to the principles and on which the negotiations were going to take place. The other is done more than three years after, after a violent war among the communities, and you have to go almost area by area to -- to see how things evolved. So I -- I don't think they are exactly comparable. The -- that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't think there were comparable either, sir, but I was just responding to the portion of the statement that indicated the results were the essentially the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the interests of time, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you tendering the two maps?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am tendering those maps, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two maps. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 17597 receives Exhibit number P7772. 65 ter number 17892 receives Exhibit number P7773, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are admitted into evidence. Before we continue ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you had indicated that 65 ter 02388 you will ask that it be added to P3076. Are you abandoning that or are you still going to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm certainly not abandoning tendering it, Your Honour, but that if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You asked that it -- you said you will ask that it be added to P3076.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, you're right. I moved ahead. So that still remains my request. We still need to upload it in that excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, I noticed that in relation to paragraph 28, 65 ter number 1D02721, which is on your list of associated exhibits, was dealt with in comparison with the letter which was sent in return which is now P7767. Having heard the witness about it and portions of letter to have been read to him, would you consider to tender that document not as an associated exhibit but in relation to the -- if do you it now, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's where a reference is made to the promises where the witness has answered to that. Madam Registrar, for 65 ter number 1D02721, what number would be assigned to it? A D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1372, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1372 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, while we're still on exhibits, I can update. I'm withdrawing two of the associated exhibits, 1D04316 and 1D04309. When we take all that into account with those that have become exhibits by other means, we're now down to ten associated exhibits, and I would thus tender those ten under Your Honours' previous guidance of associated exhibits for statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider that request. We have to make a list and provisionally --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And numbers should be assigned while we're still considering admission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I will be very short and we should finish today. I'd like to call up --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- I'd like to call up P4580 this was a document that should be in the Prosecution's binder as it was used today, and we'll need page 14 in the English, page 18 in the Serbian, and to refresh your recollection this should be the 18 March 1992 Serbian Assembly --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, in the interests of time, the entirety of the assembly sessions were not transported for the videolink but the intended excerpt, so it may or may not be that the particular portion you have in mind is in the binder, and I wanted to let you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that. It's the next few lines from where you read so I'm hoping it's there. If not, I can read it. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's not there, you can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I will read it for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right after the part that Mr. Tieger read, Mr. Karadzic went on to say as follows: "I also realised that the SDA became aware that they would know they have been defeated if they accept the idea of three national states and they tried to wiggle out of it but without much success in the army issue or any other matter. "Many issues remain unsolved such as the economy and other things. We started all, but finished nothing. If we work hard, and remain strong and stable, I hope that we can have many functions existing in the national entities and not accepting anything as final until we reach our goal. That is why your suggestions are very welcome. "If I may say this, I was much more pleased after these talks than I was after Brussels because I sensed that they understood this Assembly was the one making final decisions, not the European community." And he says: "These are my impressions." Do any of those contradict what was planned in regard to the Statement of Principles, that is to say, that there still remained work to do be done regarding the economy, and other things, the army issue, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It is perfectly acceptable, I think. It implies exactly that we have to work more and a lot in different things but that the basis is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were asked multiple times today about excerpts that various Serb politicians said at various political gatherings. I'd like to look at another document from the Prosecution's binder. It should be the last one in the binder. It's 65 ter number 33529, and it is the transcript of your testimony from the Karadzic case. And I would first ask for --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It should be the first tab in that binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. So the first tab in the binder. And I would ask for page 18 which should correlate to transcript page 33958 of the Karadzic transcript which will be visible, I believe on the upper right-hand corner, if I -- it's either on the right or the top left. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you on that page, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would then direct your attention to the answer -- or excuse me, the question and answer at lines 2 through 7. The question was: "And it's destruction of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state was not consistent with the agreement in principles, was it? "A. You cannot take bits of political discourse during some kind of meeting of an Assembly from one side or the other and present them. When I see that, I'm not surprised by that. I think the three sides had a discourse that was complicated with their own basis, if you want to --" And then you were interrupted. The first question: Do you stand by this part of what you said in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now -- and now, Ambassador, if could you, please, I give you the opportunity to finish the answer that was cut off in the Karadzic case, if you feel that you need to.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Well, the three sides had to negotiate on one side with us, the negotiators, Lord Carrington, others, myself, and to their own basis, to their own followers. And sometimes in -- that negotiation must have been difficult to all of them. We have gone today through things that, for instance, President Izetbegovic said to his people and that, at the same time, he told me that I shouldn't take that into account, that it was what he told to me that was important. And, mutatis mutandis, a bit happened like that, with the Serbs. And I suspect that the Croat negotiator [indiscernible], difficulties with his basis, particularly in western Herzegovina. So I find it perfectly normal that the kind of discussions that we read today or heard read today from the Serbian Assembly would happen, and I -- I'm sure they did happen in the equivalent bodies that discussed what the positions of the negotiators would come. I must tell you that the first time that Dr. Karadzic told me that he might agree in principle but he had to see that with his people, I thought he was trying to gain time. But then, as we went on, I realised that he did go, indeed, to his people. And sometimes what his people told him were not the things that he needed or that he wanted to negotiate capably with both the other two parts and with the internationals, in our case, the European community, later on in -- possibly in the conference with -- the Vance and Owen conference with the United Nations and the European communities. So this is all I have to say. I am not -- I'm not startled by some of the contradictions that we find in these kind of parliamentary discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question I have relates to page 23 of this same document, the transcript, and it should be page 33963 of the Karadzic transcript, and I'd like to look at lines 18 -- should be 8 through 14, I apologise. And your answer here is recorded as -- and this is the reference to the book of the aide-de-camp or chef de cabinet of Dr. Karadzic. And your answer is: "Certainly. Neither Henry Darwin or myself would have accepted ethnical cleansing to -- either by Serbs or, for that matter, by Croats or by whoever. The idea was that this will not be done, and to us in the conference, I think it was Dr. Karadzic himself who agreed that if we came to a final solution of that, there would be -- people would be -- that would have been thrown out from their places would come back to those places." Do you stand by this part of the Karadzic testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said at the time, referring to what I knew and what had happened in 1992, and I stand, indeed, to -- for what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I thank you wholeheartedly for your time and your consideration and for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am complete.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we invite Mr. Tieger or ask Mr. Tieger whether he has any further questions, I would have one question for you, Mr. Cutileiro. I think, if I understood you well, it is your opinion that if all parties would have stood by the agreement on principles that quite many lives would have been saved. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- one has to understand how things work there. We have agreed on principles. They would have had to negotiate according -- following those principles, and then, then many thousands of lives would have been saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be my next question. Your expectation of how lives would have been saved did depend on your expectation that the parties would, in a loyal sense, implement what they had agreed upon in principle and perhaps later in more detail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. Otherwise there was no point in negotiating with anybody, if you don't expect them to do as they said. It's a bit frustrating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understand your testimony to be that if the war could have been stopped that it would have saved lives at that point in time, and you had a positive expectation that war more likely would have stopped or even not started if the general principle agreement would have -- was standing. Have you -- in the loss of lives, have you considered only or primarily the -- the victims of warfare, or have you also included in your expectations the possible victims of criminal or war crimes or crime against humanity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that in some parts of the war that went on there, as you know, Your Honour, sitting where you sit, that war was -- was full of violations of human rights and laws of war, and I don't think I -- in my mind I saw it separately. I didn't see, on one hand, people legally killed and people unlegally [sic] killed, as it were. What I do think is that if they have -- if they had continued negotiating, representing the principles, there would be -- there would have been less war and therefore less malpractices during the war itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Tieger, any questions for Mr. Cutileiro?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cutileiro, this then concludes your testimony unless the Defence would have any follow-up questions on the questions of the Bench, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing. This then concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the videolink location and for having answered during quite a number of hours all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, some put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I would like to thank you specifically because I think that with -- without your steering, we might not have finished today, and I'm very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's the first time, Mr. Cutileiro, that a witness praises me for these kinds of things; I start blushing a bit perhaps. But I think everyone in this courtroom is happy that we could conclude this day. And I have to aid immediately that all that steering doesn't help if the parties are not fully co-operative. So I share the praise with the parties, if you would not mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't mind at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We should thank our hosts on the other end, the Portuguese authorities who provided the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- we are -- We'd like to thank you as well for your presence being representative of the -- Ms. Moniz, of the Portuguese government, and I do understand that the Portuguese government has provided its support and provided the facilities for the establishment of the videolink, which is highly appreciated by this Chamber and by this Tribunal. Thank you very much for that. And we can conclude the videolink.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for assisting me, Mr. Ivetic. I must admit that I was not fully aware of how the videolink was organised. So thank you very much for reminding me of that aspect. There's one decision I would very much like to read before we adjourn, and since I received information that an examination that would not go beyond 20 minutes of the usual time would still be acceptable, I abuse that now for reading a decision, which is a decision on the expertise of Dusan Pavlovic. On the 5th of October of this year, the Defence filed a notice of disclosure of Dusan Pavlovic's expert report pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 2nd of November, the Prosecution filed its notice pursuant to Rule 94 bis (B) of the Rules in which it challenged the status of Pavlovic as an expert in tracing, exhumation and identification of victims of war. The Prosecution argues that the witness's CV does not support his qualification as an expert and that his report does not demonstrate his expertise in the claimed field. The Prosecution further argues that if the Chamber qualifies the witness as an expert, it would not accept the conclusions of his report and would therefore wish to cross-examine him. On the 13th of November, the Defence filed a submission providing further details on the witness's work experience in his claimed field of expertise, while not objecting to the Prosecution's request to cross-examine the witness. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October, 2012 decision concerning Richard Butler. In relation to the Prosecution's argument that the witness does not qualify as an expert in the field of tracing, exhumation and identification of victims of war, based on the Chamber's reasoning in the decision on the expertise of witness Milan Tutoric on 22 May 2015, the Chamber considers the current situation to be distinct from the situation of Milan Tutoric's claimed expertise. Pavlovic's curriculum vitae and the submissions by the Defence show that he has work experience in the field of tracing, exhumation and identification of victims of war. In particular, Pavlovic worked for five and a half years as the head of tracing and exhumation and identification sector of the central records of missing persons in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Missing Persons Institute and is currently employed as a senior associate for exhumation, forensic processing, identification, records, and field-work related to the search of missing persons for the Republika Srpska Government Centre for Research of War, War Crimes, and Tracing Missing Persons. His responsibilities include documents and analysing the list of missing persons around Srebrenica in July 1995; proposing exhumation plans; participating in visits to graves, exhumations, and forensic analysis of remains; and drafting reports on exhumed and identified persons. While Pavlovic's expertise is not demonstrated very clearly in the Defence's submissions, there is a sufficient basis for the Chamber to accept that he has specialised knowledge and expertise in tracing, exhumation, and identification of victims of war and that such knowledge and expertise may be of assistance to the Chamber in assessing the evidence presented by the parties -- by both parties. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, that Pavlovic may be called to testify as an expert witness in the fields of tracing, exhumation and identification of victims of war and that he shall be made available for cross-examination. Concerning the arguments related to the methodology of Pavlovic's report, the Chamber considers that these are matters that can and should be addressed during the examination of this witness. Therefore, the Chamber defers its decision on the admission of his report until the time of his testimony. The Chamber now directs the Defence's attention to one further observation concerning Pavlovic's report. In his report, Pavlovic includes to a large extent expert opinion which appears to fall outside the scope of his area of expertise. Many pages of the report focus on the political and military situation in Srebrenica between 1993 and 1995. Further, the witness offers conclusions related to the ethnic cleansing of Serbs and genocide, which, again, seem to be outside the scope of his expertise. In addition, the witness evaluates evidentiary materials, including statements and testimonies of witnesses. The report does not fully reveal what evidentiary material Pavlovic has reviewed or whether such material is in evidence. On that basis, the witness then draws conclusions not covered by his field of expertise. The Chamber emphasises that it allows Pavlovic to be called in his capacity as an expert in tracing, exhumation and identification of victims of war but not as an expert in history, law, military matters, or any other field for which he is not qualified. The Chamber therefore expects the parties to focus their examination of the witness on those aspects of the report that relate to the witness's area of expertise. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Before we adjourn, I'd like to thank very much all those assisting us that they enabled us -- I should have extended the praise to you as well and not only to the parties but that enabled us to conclude hearing the testimony of Mr. Cutileiro today. It is, as always, highly appreciated by the Chamber. We adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 10th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
